sentences.text: Maiaspondylus is an extinct genus of ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaurs found in Canada, England, and Russia. The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is distinguished from other ichthyosaurs by extensive overlapping contact between the jugal and maxilla bones.
Its teeth feature smooth crowns, striated cement, lingual curvature, and implantation in a dental groove.
The humerus has isomorphic proximal and distal ends with three distal articular facets, where the medial facet is smaller than the lateral ones.
The embryos found in Maiaspondylus are the geologically youngest and physically smallest known ichthyosaur embryos.
Referred materials include two articulated embryos found within the body cavity of an adult skeleton.

The genus is known from a nearly complete, disarticulated holotype skeleton preserved in three dimensions. All specimens were collected at Hay River from the Loon River Formation, dating to about 110 million years ago.

The genus was named by Maxwell and Caldwell in 2006, with the type species being Maiaspondylus lindoei. The generic name combines Greek words for "caring mother" and "vertebra", while the specific name honors technician Allan Lindoe for discovering and preparing the specimens.
Researchers suggested that the presence of embryos inside an adult proves Maiaspondylus was viviparous, giving live birth.
Specimens were originally referred to Platypterygius, but recent cladistic analyses confirm Maiaspondylus is a valid ophthalmosaurid genus.
Druckenmiller and Maxwell (2010) found Maiaspondylus most closely related to a species of Platypterygius that likely does not belong to that genus.
Maiaspondylus lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.
